strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed clothing addresses a useful retrieval setting. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets.

The reported improvements are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.91% Rank-1 and 55.63% mAP, compared with 35.38% and 44.08% for the strongest reported non-Word4Per comparator in Table I.
The two-stage method is coherent and practical. It uses existing person image-text supervision to adapt CLIP, then trains a lightweight mapping network without CPR training triplets.

The experiments examine two backbones, alternative supervision, data quantities, network architectures, prompts, and ensembles. Training settings and timing measurements provide useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The main comparison does not adequately isolate the contribution. Table I and Section V-B state that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with the original CLIP, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This creates an encoder–mapping compatibility confound that the authors acknowledge but do not resolve. Retraining these baselines with the same adapted encoders and person images is essential to establish improvements beyond domain adaptation.

Methodological originality is limited: image-to-pseudo-word mapping and composed prompting closely follow Pic2Word/SEARLE, while the encoder adaptation uses established similarity-distribution and identity losses. Caption supervision is a potentially useful extension, but the claimed explanation involving foreground emphasis remains weakly supported. Figure 9 visualizes the visual encoder frozen before TINet training and therefore cannot itself establish what different TINet objectives retain or discard.

The evaluation and model-selection protocol is unclear. ITCPR is described as exclusively a test set, yet architectures, hidden widths, prompts, and ensemble configurations are chosen through experiments on it. No separate validation protocol is described. This does not establish that CPR triplets trained the network weights, but it leaves the reported generalization performance vulnerable to test-set selection.

The benchmark's annotation reliability needs stronger support. False-negative correction relies on visually retrieved top-k candidates, but the retrieval encoder, k, annotation agreement, and residual-error audit are not specified. Inspecting retrieved candidates does not establish that all relevant gallery images have been found, which directly affects mAP. Results broken down by source dataset and clothing-change type would also help establish the benchmark's coverage.

Some reporting gaps hinder reproducibility and interpretation. The text following Table V selects configuration 4, whereas Section III-C specifies the template in configuration 5. The ensemble description also leaves ambiguity between averaging pseudo-word embeddings and encoded query representations. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, making the smaller differences between objectives, prompts, and ensembles difficult to assess.

Ethical documentation is incomplete for a system intended to identify people across clothing changes. The manuscript does not explain the permission and consent conditions governing reuse of the person images or discuss privacy, surveillance misuse, and demographic performance limitations. Public availability of the source datasets does not by itself resolve these questions.
